keeping tools clean and returning them after use

questions.stem: Kente cloth worn by chiefs in Ghana mainly expresses
options: the military rank of the wearer only
questions.explanation: Patterns and colours of kente carry meanings linked to status, history and identity.

questions.stem: Wool is obtained from
options: the seed hair of a plant
questions.explanation: Wool is a protein fibre from sheep's fleece.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a bast (stem) fibre?
questions.explanation: Bast fibres such as jute and flax come from plant stems.

questions.stem: Washing raw wool to remove grease, dirt and suint is called
questions.explanation: Scouring cleans raw wool; the grease recovered is lanolin.

questions.stem: Removing the gum (sericin) from raw silk to make it soft and lustrous is
questions.explanation: Degumming dissolves the sericin that binds silk filaments.

questions.stem: The process that disentangles fibres and arranges them roughly parallel into a web or sliver is
questions.explanation: Carding opens and aligns fibres before spinning.

questions.stem: A long continuous strand such as silk or nylon, as opposed to short fibres, is described as
questions.explanation: Filaments are continuous; staple fibres are short lengths.

questions.stem: Polyester fabric is best dyed with
questions.explanation: Hydrophobic polyester is dyed with disperse dyes at high temperature.

questions.explanation: A mixture uses different yarns in warp and weft; a blend mixes fibres within one yarn.

questions.stem: The traditional Yoruba aso oke is woven on a
options: broad vertical loom used by women
questions.explanation: Aso oke is woven in narrow strips by men on horizontal looms and sewn together.

questions.stem: In a weave plan drawn on point paper, a filled square usually indicates that
options: the fabric is to be knitted afterwards
the warp is lifted over the weft
questions.explanation: Filled squares show warp over weft; blank squares show weft over warp.

questions.stem: A variation of plain weave in which two or more threads work together as one is
questions.explanation: Basket (hopsack) weave doubles the threads of plain weave.

questions.stem: Passing warp ends through the dents of the reed is
questions.explanation: Denting (sleying) threads ends through the reed.

questions.stem: Let-off and take-up are classified as
questions.explanation: Secondary motions control release of warp and winding of cloth.

questions.stem: A loom that inserts the weft with jets of air instead of a shuttle is a
questions.explanation: Air-jet, water-jet, rapier and projectile looms are shuttleless.

In knitted fabric, a vertical column of loops is called a

questions.stem: Fabric produced from fibres held together by adhesive, heat or needle punching without yarns is
questions.explanation: Non-wovens are made directly from fibre webs.

questions.stem: Common salt is added to a direct dye bath mainly to
options: help the dye move onto the fibre
change the colour of the dye
remove wax from the fabric surface quickly
questions.explanation: Salt acts as an exhausting agent, driving dye onto cellulose fibres.

questions.stem: Removing colour from a dyed fabric in selected areas to create white patterns is
questions.explanation: Discharge printing uses chemicals to bleach out colour in pattern areas.

questions.stem: Cutting shapes of fabric and stitching them onto a background fabric is
questions.explanation: Appliqué applies fabric shapes to a ground.

questions.stem: Burning off protruding surface fibres to give cotton a smooth surface is
questions.explanation: Singeing passes fabric over flames or hot plates.

questions.stem: A mechanical finish that compresses cotton fabric so it will not shrink much during washing is
questions.explanation: Sanforising is controlled compressive pre-shrinking.

questions.stem: On a care label, a triangle symbol refers to
questions.explanation: A triangle is the bleaching symbol; a tub is washing; an iron is ironing; a circle is dry cleaning.

questions.stem: Using traditional motifs such as the Adinkra symbols of Ghana in a fabric design mainly
questions.explanation: Indigenous motifs carry cultural messages and identity.

questions.stem: Which practice reduces waste in a textile workshop?
questions.explanation: Reusing offcuts in patchwork or appliqué reduces waste.

questions.stem: Waste dye water from a dyeing workshop should be
options: stored in open pits near homes
questions.explanation: Untreated dye effluent pollutes water and soil.

questions.stem: A major challenge facing the Nigerian textile industry is
options: lack of land suitable for growing cotton
high cost of power and production
questions.explanation: Unreliable power and high production costs, plus imports, have weakened local mills.

questions.explanation: Travelling exhibitions tour several venues.

questions.explanation: Catalogues document exhibited works.

questions.explanation: Attractive packaging promotes sales.

questions.stem:
(a) Describe the processing of raw cotton from harvesting to yarn. [9 marks]
(b) Distinguish between a single yarn, a ply yarn and a cable yarn. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
2 marks: Harvesting/picking ripe bolls and drying
2 marks: Ginning to separate fibres from seeds
2 marks: Opening, cleaning and carding to align the fibres into sliver
2 marks: Drawing and roving to make the strand uniform and thinner
1 mark: Spinning, inserting twist to form yarn
2 marks: Single yarn: one strand of twisted fibres
2 marks: Ply yarn: two or more single yarns twisted together
2 marks: Cable yarn: two or more ply yarns twisted together
questions.explanation: Cotton is picked, ginned, cleaned and carded, drawn and roved, then spun. A single yarn is one strand; ply yarns twist singles together; cable yarns twist plies together.

questions.stem:
(a) Name and explain the three primary motions of a loom. [9 marks]
(b) State three differences between the traditional narrow loom and the broad loom. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Shedding: raising some warp ends and lowering others to make an opening (shed)
3 marks: Picking: passing the weft through the shed with a shuttle or other carrier
3 marks: Beating-up: pushing the inserted weft into the fell of the cloth with the reed or beater
2 marks: Narrow loom produces narrow strips; broad loom produces wide cloth
2 marks: Narrow loom usually horizontal and operated by men; broad loom often vertical/upright and traditionally operated by women
2 marks: Narrow loom uses treadles and pulleys; broad loom uses fixed beams with a heddle rod and shed stick
questions.explanation: Primary motions are shedding, picking and beating-up. The narrow loom gives strips (aso oke, kente) and is worked by men with treadles; the broad loom gives wider cloth (akwete) and is upright, worked by women.

questions.stem:
A handwoven stole is to be 2 m long and 0.4 m wide, with 15 ends per cm and 12 picks per cm. Ignoring wastage:
(a) calculate the number of warp ends; [3 marks]
(b) calculate the total length of warp yarn; [3 marks]
(c) calculate the number of picks and the total length of weft yarn; [6 marks]
(d) state three causes of wastage in weaving. [3 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Ends = 40 cm x 15 = 600 ends
3 marks: Warp length = 600 x 2 m = 1,200 m
3 marks: Picks = 200 cm x 12 = 2,400 picks
3 marks: Weft length = 2,400 x 0.4 m = 960 m
1 mark: Loom waste at the start and end of the warp
1 mark: Take-up of yarn through interlacing
1 mark: Broken ends, knots and fringes
questions.explanation: 600 ends of 2 m give 1,200 m of warp; 2,400 picks of 0.4 m give 960 m of weft. Real requirements are higher because of loom waste, take-up and breakages.

questions.stem:
(a) List five materials needed for batik. [5 marks]
(b) Describe the steps in producing a two-colour batik. [10 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
1 mark: Cotton fabric
1 mark: Wax (paraffin and beeswax)
1 mark: Tjanting or brush
1 mark: Dyes and dye bath
1 mark: Wax pot/heater, frame, iron and newsprint
2 marks: Wash, dry and iron the fabric; transfer the design
2 marks: Apply hot wax to areas to remain white
2 marks: Dye in the lighter colour, rinse and dry
2 marks: Wax areas to keep the first colour and dye in the darker colour
2 marks: Remove wax by ironing between newsprint or boiling, then wash and finish
questions.explanation: Batik uses fabric, wax, tjanting, dyes and a heater. Wax the white areas, dye light, wax again, dye dark, then remove wax by ironing or boiling.

questions.stem:
(a) Explain the following finishes: (i) bleaching (ii) waterproofing (iii) napping. [9 marks]
(b) State three ways of caring for a printed cotton fabric. [6 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: Bleaching: chemical treatment to remove natural colour and make fabric white
3 marks: Waterproofing: coating or treating fabric so water cannot penetrate
3 marks: Napping: brushing the surface to raise fibre ends for softness and warmth
2 marks: Wash with mild soap in warm water, inside out
2 marks: Dry in shade to prevent fading
2 marks: Iron on the reverse at the correct temperature and store clean and dry
questions.explanation: Bleaching whitens; waterproofing repels water; napping raises a soft surface. Printed cotton should be washed gently, dried in shade and ironed on the reverse.

questions.stem:
(a) What is an exhibition? [3 marks]
(b) Describe four stages in mounting an exhibition of textile works. [8 marks]
(c) State two reasons why an artist should keep a portfolio. [4 marks]
questions.markingGuide:
3 marks: A public display of works for viewing, appreciation, promotion and sale
2 marks: Planning: theme, budget, date and venue
2 marks: Selection, labelling and pricing of works
2 marks: Publicity: invitations, posters, catalogue, media
2 marks: Mounting, opening ceremony and evaluation afterwards
2 marks: To show skills and range of work to clients, employers or examiners
2 marks: To record progress and preserve works for reference
questions.explanation: An exhibition displays works publicly. Stages: plan, select and label, publicise, mount, open and evaluate. A portfolio showcases skill and records growth.
